summary: Queue depth climbed for 27 minutes with arrival rate normal and consumer throughput down ~40%, so the stall is on the consumption side rather than a load surge. Two candidate causes were introduced in the preceding hour (a consumer-library upgrade and a database index rebuild), and consumer logs show symptoms consistent with each (lock waits and deserialization warnings). Because both changes were reverted together and no single-change revert exists, the evidence supports 'one or both of these changes degraded consumption' but cannot apportion blame between them. Missing per-phase timing telemetry and absent traces make the two mechanisms indistinguishable in the retained data.

claims.text: The backlog grew from reduced consumption, not from increased input: arrival rate stayed in the normal range while queue depth rose for 27 minutes.
Consumer throughput dropped roughly 40% over the same interval as the queue growth.
At least one of the two preceding changes (consumer-library upgrade, database index rebuild) is causally implicated, since reverting both restored throughput.
The evidence does not determine which change caused the degradation, or whether both contributed; the joint revert confounds the two.
Two distinct degradation mechanisms are simultaneously visible in consumer logs: increased lock waiting and increased deserialization retries/warnings.

Lock-wait messages are the symptom class more naturally associated with the database index rebuild, and deserialization warnings with the consumer-library upgrade, but the case package supplies no evidence linking either symptom to either change.
Retained telemetry cannot attribute consumer processing time between database waiting and deserialization retrying.
No trace samples survive from the incident window, so the per-message time breakdown cannot be reconstructed after the fact.
Restoration of throughput after the joint revert is consistent with the changes being causal, but is also consistent with coincidental recovery; no control period is documented.
The incident is currently mitigated: throughput returned to normal after the revert.

relationships.rationale: Normal arrival with falling throughput identifies the consumer side as the constrained stage.
A ~40% throughput drop mechanically produces steady queue growth at constant arrival.
Both changes landed within the hour before the observed stall.
Revert-and-recover links the change set to the throughput loss.
Lock waiting and deserialization retries are plausible time sinks between change and throughput loss, though their shares are unmeasured.
Without split processing-time telemetry, the competing mechanisms cannot be separated.
Absent traces remove the retrospective route to attribution.
The absence of a single-change revert run leaves the two interventions fully confounded.
Symptom-to-change mapping is an unsupported inference within this evidence set.
Recovery on revert is the only causal test present in the package.
Lack of a control weakens the inference that the changes, rather than time, explain recovery.

uncertainties.text: Which of the two changes, or which combination, caused the throughput loss.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: A staged re-application or single-change revert run: restore one change at a time and observe throughput and queue depth.

uncertainties.text: How consumer processing time divided between database lock waiting and deserialization retrying.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Per-phase timing instrumentation in the consumer that reports database-wait and deserialization time as separate metrics.

uncertainties.text: Whether the two logged symptom classes are independent effects or one drives the other (e.g. retries lengthening transactions and increasing lock contention).
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Retained distributed traces or correlated per-message logs showing ordering of deserialization retries and lock acquisition.

uncertainties.text: Whether lock waits were caused by the index rebuild specifically, or by some other database activity in the window.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Database-side lock and maintenance-operation logs covering the incident window.

uncertainties.text: Whether the ~40% throughput drop is fully explained by these two symptom classes, or whether an unmeasured third factor contributed.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: A time budget accounting for total consumer processing time across all phases during a reproduction.

uncertainties.text: Whether recovery after the joint revert was caused by the revert or coincided with an independent change in conditions.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: A documented control interval, or reproduction of the degradation by re-applying the change set.

uncertainties.text: Whether the log message increases were proportionate to the throughput loss or merely present; magnitudes are not quantified in the evidence.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Message-rate counts for lock-wait and deserialization warnings, baseline versus incident window.

actions.text: Re-apply the two changes one at a time in a non-production or shadow environment to break the confound and identify the responsible change.
Add separate consumer metrics for database-wait time and deserialization time per message before any re-application.
Restore and retain trace sampling with a retention window that outlives incident investigation.
Collect database-side lock and maintenance logs for the incident window to test the index-rebuild hypothesis directly.
Quantify the baseline-versus-incident rates of both log message classes rather than relying on the qualitative 'increased'.
Adopt a change policy that separates consumer-library upgrades from database maintenance windows so future reverts are attributable.

counterfactuals.text: If a run existed in which only the library upgrade was reverted, throughput behavior in that run would identify or exonerate the upgrade.
If telemetry had separated database-wait from deserialization-retry time, the dominant mechanism could be identified without any revert experiment.
If traces from the incident window had been retained, per-message time breakdowns could have been reconstructed retrospectively.
If arrival rate had risen instead of staying normal, the backlog would be explainable as load rather than consumer degradation, and the two changes would not be implicated.
If throughput had not recovered after the joint revert, both changes would be largely exonerated and an unidentified third factor would be indicated.
If only one symptom class had appeared in the logs, the mapping from symptom to change would be less ambiguous even without additional telemetry.
